n: After his prayer, Jesus leads the disciples across the Kidron Valley to a garden on the Mount of Olives — Gethsemane, as the other Gospels name it. There he would suffer for the sins of the world.

f.g: The Kidron, a seasonal stream east of Jerusalem; David crossed it weeping when fleeing Absalom.

n: Judas knew the place because Jesus often went there with his disciples. Jesus didn’t hide; he went where he could be found.

f.g: ofttimes = often; resorted thither = went there.

n: Judas arrives with a detachment of soldiers and temple police sent by the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons — coming with artificial lights to seize the Light of the World.

f.g: A Roman cohort (or part of one) — showing Roman involvement from the start.

n: Fully aware of what is coming, Jesus steps forward to meet them and asks, “Who are you looking for?” He is in control, not the mob.

f.w: knowing all things that should come upon him

n: They say, “Jesus of Nazareth.” He answers, “I am he” — again “I am.” John notes that Judas is standing with the arresting party.

f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

n: At his words “I am,” the soldiers draw back and fall to the ground — a brief glimpse of his divine power, even as he submits to arrest.

f.w: they went backward, and fell to the ground

n: He asks again whom they seek, and again they answer, “Jesus of Nazareth.”
He repeats that he is the one, and asks them to let his disciples go. Even as he is arrested, he protects his own.
This fulfilled his own words in his prayer that he had lost none of those the Father gave him.

f.w: Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none

n: Peter draws a sword and strikes the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear. Only John names the two men — Peter and Malchus.

f.g: Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

n: Jesus tells Peter to put the sword away: shouldn’t he drink the cup the Father has given him? He goes to his suffering willingly.

f.w: the cup which my Father hath given me

n: The soldiers, their commander, and the temple officers seize Jesus and tie him up.

f.g: Greek chiliarchos — a Roman tribune, commander of about a thousand soldiers.

n: They take him first to Annas, father-in-law of the current high priest Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest earlier and still held great influence.

f.g: High priest about AD 6–15; five of his sons later held the office as well.

n: John reminds readers that Caiaphas is the one who advised that one man should die for the people.

f.w: it was expedient that one man should die for the people

n: Peter follows, along with another disciple — likely John — who knew the high priest and so got into the courtyard with Jesus.

f.g: Unnamed, but often identified with the beloved disciple (John 20:2).
palace = the courtyard of the high priest’s residence.

n: Peter waits outside the gate until the other disciple speaks to the girl at the door and brings him in.

f.g: A servant girl acting as doorkeeper.

n: The doorkeeper asks Peter if he’s one of “this man’s” disciples too. Peter says, “I am not” — his first denial, in contrast to Jesus’s “I am.”

f.g: damsel = young woman, servant girl.

n: It is a cold night, and servants and officers stand around a charcoal fire. Peter stands with them, warming himself — among the very people who arrested Jesus.

f.g: A charcoal fire; John mentions one again in John 21:9, when Peter is restored.

n: The high priest questions Jesus about his disciples and his teaching, hoping to find something to charge him with.

f.g: doctrine = teaching.

n: Jesus replies that he has always taught openly in synagogues and the temple; he has said nothing in secret.

f.w: I spake openly to the world

n: Why question him? Under their own legal practice, witnesses should be heard. Ask those who listened to him.

f.g: Jewish law did not require an accused man to testify against himself; the case should rest on witnesses.

n: An officer slaps Jesus for speaking that way to the high priest.

f.w: struck Jesus with the palm of his hand

n: Jesus calmly answers: if he said something wrong, testify to what it was; if not, why strike him? He insists on justice without retaliating.

f.g: smitest = hit, strike.

n: Annas then sends Jesus, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.

f.g: John skips the trial before Caiaphas that the other Gospels record.

n: Meanwhile Peter is still warming himself by the fire. Asked again if he is a disciple, he denies it a second time.
A relative of Malchus — whose ear Peter cut off — asks if he didn’t see Peter in the garden with Jesus. The danger is very personal now.

f.w: his kinsman whose ear Peter cut off
f.g: kinsman = relative.

n: Peter denies a third time, and at that moment a rooster crows — just as Jesus foretold.

f.g: Luke adds that Jesus looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.

n: At dawn they take Jesus from Caiaphas to the Roman governor’s headquarters. The accusers won’t enter a Gentile’s house, to avoid becoming ritually unclean before the Passover meal — careful about ritual while plotting an innocent man’s death.

f.g: The praetorium, the Roman governor’s residence and court in Jerusalem.

n: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, comes out to them and asks what charge they bring.

f.g: Roman prefect of Judea about AD 26–36, known for harsh treatment of the Jews.

n: They evade the question: if he weren’t a criminal, they wouldn’t have brought him.

f.g: malefactor = evildoer, criminal.

n: Pilate tells them to judge him by their own law. They reply that they aren’t allowed to execute anyone — revealing that they want him dead.

f.w: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death
f.g: Under Roman rule, the Jewish council generally lacked authority to carry out capital punishment.

n: This fulfilled Jesus’s own prediction of how he would die: lifted up on a Roman cross, rather than stoned under Jewish law.

f.w: signifying what death he should die

n: Pilate goes back inside, summons Jesus, and asks, “Are you the King of the Jews?” — the political charge that could mean rebellion against Rome.

f.w: Art thou the King of the Jews?

n: Jesus asks whether Pilate means this himself or is repeating what others said.

f.w: Sayest thou this thing of thyself
f.g: In effect: is this your question, or theirs?

n: Pilate scoffs, “Am I a Jew?” His own people and chief priests handed him over — what has he done?

f.g: Pilate distances himself from what he sees as an internal Jewish dispute.

n: Jesus explains his kingdom isn’t of this world. If it were, his followers would fight to stop his arrest. His is a kingdom of truth and hearts, not armies.

f.w: My kingdom is not of this world

n: “So you are a king?” Pilate asks. Jesus answers that Pilate has said it, and explains he was born to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who loves truth listens to him.

f.w: To this end was I born
Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice

n: Pilate asks, “What is truth?” — perhaps cynically — and walks away without waiting for an answer, though Truth stands before him. He then declares Jesus innocent.

f.w: I find in him no fault at all

n: Pilate reminds them of a Passover custom of releasing one prisoner, and offers to free “the King of the Jews.”
The crowd shouts for Barabbas instead — a robber and insurrectionist. The guilty man goes free while the innocent one is condemned, a picture of what Christ does for us all.

f.g: Aramaic for “son of the father.” Mark and Luke say he took part in a rebellion and committed murder.
